title: WPMS/2590/2017 of Uttarakhand Van Vikas Nigam Karmachari Sangthan Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 2590 of 2017
Uttarakhand Van Vikas Nigam
Karmachari Sangthan Ö Petitioner
Vs
State of Uttarakhand & others Ö Respondents
Mr. Shobhit Saharia, Mr. Yogesh Pacholia and Mr. N.S. Kanyal, Advocates for the petitioner.
Mr. N.S. Pundir, Deputy Advocate General for the State.
Mr. Rakesh Thapliyal, Advocate assisted by Mr. V.K. Kaparwan, Advocate for respondent Nos. 2 to 6.
Honíble Manoj K. Tiwari, J. (Oral)
 This writ petition has been filed by Trade Union of
Employees of Uttarakhand Forest Development Corporation
(hereinafter referred to as ëthe Corporationí). They are challenging
a policy decision taken by the Corporation to outsource the work
of supply, installation, operation and maintenance of Electronic
Weighing Bridges across various gates of River Gaula in District
Nainital, on various grounds.
2. Uttarakhand Forest Development Corporation is a
statutory body created under Uttarakhand Forest Corporation
Act and the Central Government has granted permission to the
said Corporation to pick river bed material from River Gaula.
3. Petitioner is aggrieved by the policy decision taken by
the Corporation to award contract of operation and maintenance
of Electronic Weighing Bridges across different gates of Gaula
River. This decision, according to the petitioner, is unwise as it
will result in loss of revenue to the Corporation. Thus, according
to the petitioner, the Corporation should establish Electronic
Weighing Bridges which may be operated through its employees.
It is further the contention of the petitioner that the impugned
decision is contrary to the Mining Policy contained in
Government Order dated 30.04.2001 which prohibits the
Corporation from subletting the work of picking river bed
material, to other persons.

2
4. Regarding the question of locus standi, submission of
the petitioner is that since members of the petitioner are getting
salary and other benefits out of the funds of the Corporation,
therefore, the impugned decision has direct bearing upon its
members. The relief sought by the petitioner in this writ petition
is extracted below:-
ìI. Issue a writ, rule, order or direction in the nature of certiorari calling for
records and to quash the decision of respondent authorities (Copy of aforesaid
decision is not given to petitioner) of corporation to install the Weighing
Machine through private operators in the gates of river from where miner
minerals are being carried out through the trucks, because due to the
aforesaid decision of the corporation, the Government has to bare substantial
revenue loss and this act of authorities is in gross violation of the mining policy
issued by Government of Uttarakhand in the year 2001 by which the work of
collecting the mines and minerals from the reserve forest area was allotted to
Uttarakhand Forest Development Corporation.
II. Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of Mandamus commanding and
directing the respondents to not to act upon its earlier decision and take all the
activities regarding collection of minor minerals and its measurement, by its
own resources and install its own weighing machines/bridge in all the river
gates, so that the revenue of Corporation, as well as Government of
Uttarakhand may be increased and any probable revenue loss may be
reduced.î
5. A perusal of the Mining Policy of the State contained in
Government Order dated 30.04.2017 reveals that the work of
mining cannot be sublet by the Corporation. There is no
allegation in the writ petition that mining work is being sublet to
any other person. The only decision which has been taken is to
award contract for supply, operation and maintenance of
Electronic Weighing Bridges, which does not amount to
subletting of mining work. There is no allegation that contractor
will undertake the work of picking up of river bed material.
6. In my humble opinion, scope of judicial review in these
matters is very limited. This Court in exercise of power under
Article 226 of the Constitution cannot substitute its opinion with
a decision taken by the Corporation merely because it disagrees
with the decision, as held by Honíble Supreme Court in AFCONS
Infrastructure Limited Vs. Nagpur Metro Rail Corporation
Limited (2016) 16 SCC 818. Para 13 of the said judgment is
extracted below:-

3
 ì13. In other words, a mere disagreement with the decision-making process or the decision of the administrative authority is no reason for
a constitutional court to interfere. The threshold of mala-fides, intention to
favour someone or arbitrariness, irrationality or perversity must be met before
the constitutional court interferes with the decision-making process or the
decision.î
7. Even otherwise also, in my opinion, Trade Union or
Association of Employees does not have locus standi to maintain
a writ petition challenging a policy decision taken by the
employer which has no direct bearing on the employees. As a
commercial undertaking, the Corporation is free to take any
policy decision provided it is not contrary to the statute under
which the Corporation has been created or any other law holding
the field. It was open to the petitioner to give its suggestion to the
Competent Authority in the Corporation, but once a decision has
been taken to outsource the work of establishment and
maintenance of Electronic Weighing Bridges, petitioner cannot
challenge the same by filing a writ petition.
8. Learned counsel for the petitioner has relied upon a
judgment rendered by Honíble Supreme Court in the case of
Jasbhai Motibhai Desai Vs. Roshan Kumar, Haji Bashir
Ahmed and others, reported in AIR 1976 SC 578. Reliance has
been placed upon paras 36, 37 and 38 of the said judgment
which are extracted below:-
ì36. It will be seen that in the context of locus standi to apply for a writ of
certiorari, an applicant may ordinarily fall in any of these categories: (i)
ëperson aggrievedí; (ii) ëstrangerí; (iii) busybody of meddle-some interloper.
Persons in the last category are easily distinguishable from those coming
under the first two categories. Such persons interfere in things which do not
concern them. They masquerade as crusaders for justice. They pretend to act
in the name of Pro Bono Publico, though they have no interest of the public or
even of their own to protect. They indulge in the past-time of meddling with the
judicial process either by force of habit or from improper motives. Often, they
are actuated by a desire to win notoriety or cheap popularity; while the ulterior
intent of some applicants in this category may be no more than spoking the
wheels of administration. The High Court should do well to reject the
applications of such busybodies at the threshold.
37. The distinction between the first and second categories of applicants
though real, is not always well-demarcated. The first category has, as it were,
two concentric zones; a solid central zone of certainty and a grey outer circle of
lessening certainty in a sliding centrifugal scale, with an outermost nebulous
fringe of uncertainty. Applicants falling within the central zone are those

4
whose legal rights have been infringed. Such applicants undoubtedly stand in
the category of ëpersons aggrievedí. In the grey outer-circle the bounds which
separate the first category from the second, intermix, interfuse and overlap
increasingly in a centrifugal direction. All persons in this outerzone may not be
ìpersons aggrievedî.
38. To distinguish such applicants from ëstrangersí among them, some broad
tests may be deduced from the conspectus made above. These tests are not
absolute and ultimate. Their efficacy varies according to the circumstances of
the case, including the statutory context in which the matter falls to be
considered. These are: Whether the applicant is a person whose legal right
has been infringed? Has he suffered a legal wrong or injury, in the sense, that
his interest, recognized by law, has been prejudicially and directly affected by
the act or omission of the authority, complained of? Is he a person who has
suffered a legal grievance, a person ìagainst whom a decision has been
pronounced which has wrongfully deprived him of something or wrongfully
refused him something or wrongfully affected his title to something? Has he a
special and substantial grievance of his own beyond some grievance or
inconvenience suffered by him in common with the rest of the public? Was he
entitled to object and be heard by the authority before it took the impugned
action? If so, was he prejudicially affected in the exercise of that right by the
act of usurpation of jurisdiction on that part of the authority? Is the statute, in
the context of which the scope of the words ìperson aggrievedî is being
considered, a social welfare measure designed to lay down ethical or
professional standards of conduct for the community? Or is it a statute dealing
with private rights of particular individuals?
9. The aforesaid judgment relied by learned counsel for
the petitioner is distinguishable on facts as in that case, there
was a dispute between two business rivals which is not the case
here. Even otherwise also, petitioner cannot be said to be a
person aggrieved. Members of petitioner union have no personal
interest in the matter and unless their service conditions are
altered to their prejudice, they cannot maintain a writ petition
challenging a policy decision which is purely commercial in
nature.
10. In such view of the matter, I find no force in the writ
petition and the writ petition is liable to be dismissed and is
hereby dismissed.
(Manoj K. Tiwari, J.)
17.11.2017
 Ujjwal
